claims.text: The starting material is a homogeneous, single-phase refractory high-entropy alloy containing at least five elements at no less than 5 at.% each and no rare-earth elements.
Adding a small amount of terbium will modify the superconducting transition temperature of the refractory high-entropy alloy.
Terbium substitution induces local lattice distortions in the alloy matrix.
Terbium substitution introduces localized magnetic moments into the alloy matrix.
Incorporated terbium alters the local electronic environment and lattice symmetry.
Incorporated terbium changes electron-scattering profiles in the alloy.
Terbium-induced lattice perturbations may enhance electron-phonon coupling.
Localized terbium magnetic moments may cause superconducting pair breaking.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling could increase the superconducting transition temperature.
Magnetic pair breaking could suppress the superconducting transition temperature.
Keeping the terbium concentration below approximately 10 at.% may avoid phase separation and secondary magnetic phases.
At excessive terbium concentrations, phase separation or dominant magnetic ordering may occur and change the superconducting response.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution without significant segregation.
A Tb-doped sample and an undoped sample should be prepared under identical arc-melting and cooling conditions.
Phase homogeneity should be assessed by X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy.
The superconducting transition should be measured using both resistivity and magnetization.
The hypothesis is falsified if terbium addition produces no statistically significant change in transition temperature relative to the undoped control.
A transition-temperature change attributable to inhomogeneity, phase separation, or processing artifacts does not support an intrinsic terbium-alloying mechanism.
